Mihai has received an unexpected email: a big hospital in Bucharest is offering him the post of head of department. In the evening, he tells Ana.
Ana, I need to tell you something. I’ve been offered a job in Bucharest. Head of cardiology.
Head of department? That’s incredible! So what are you going to do?
I don’t know. If it were just me, I think I’d accept. But now there are two of us.
Let’s think about it. If you accepted, when would you have to start?
In January. And if we moved, we’d be close to my parents and my grandfather.
That would be lovely. Your grandfather is ninety-one… But what about my job? If I left Madrid, I’d lose my post at the school.
I know. Could you teach Spanish in Bucharest? There are secondary schools looking for native teachers.
I could, yes. But I’d have to learn Romanian. If I spoke Romanian, everything would be easier.
You already know “noroc”, “mulțumesc” and “zacuscă”. That’s a good start.
Ha-ha. On the one hand, I feel like an adventure. On the other, I’d be really sad to leave my family, my grandmother, the club…
And I’d miss Kenji, ramen, the Madrid sunshine… And Tama.
Mihai, tell me the truth. If it weren’t for me, would you go?
If it weren’t for you, I probably wouldn’t be in Madrid. I’d have left two years ago.
Then it isn’t your decision. It’s ours. How about we go to Bucharest for a week before we decide?
Sounds perfect. If you like it, we’ll think about it seriously. If you don’t, I’ll say no and that’s that.
Deal. But if I were you, I wouldn’t say anything to your mother yet. If she finds out, she’ll start looking for a flat for us tomorrow.

Make a small pause after the “si” part: «Si tuviera tiempo, | viajaría». Your voice rises on “tiempo” and falls on “viajaría”.
The stress always falls on the í: via-ha-REE-a, a-REE-a, ten-DREE-a. Don’t shorten it!

In Spanish, “si” (if) has two main uses, depending on how real the condition is:
Si llueve, me quedo en casa.
Si lloviera, me quedaría en casa.

English does the same! “If it rains, I’ll stay at home” (real) versus “If it rained, I’d stay at home” (hypothetical). Where English uses the past after “if” (if it RAINED, if I WERE), Spanish uses the imperfect subjunctive.
NEVER put the conditional after “si”! “Si tendría dinero…” is wrong (just like “if I would have money”). Correct: Si tuviera dinero, compraría… The conditional goes in the OTHER half of the sentence.
2. Hypotheses about the present: what if
If I were rich, I’d travel all over the world. (but I’m not)
If I spoke Romanian, everything would be easier. (but I don’t)
If it weren’t for you, I wouldn’t be in Madrid. (but it is you)
The order can be reversed, with no comma: Viajaría por todo el mundo si fuera rico.
The classic question in conversations and exams: ¿Qué harías si…? E.g.: ¿Qué harías si te tocara la lotería? (What would you do if you won the lottery?)
The conditional (chapter 27) is formed from the INFINITIVE + -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. The irregulars are the same as in the future:
The typical combination: si TUVIERA… TENDRÍA. Both forms come from “tener”, but by different routes: tuviera from the indefinido (tuvieron), tendría from the future (tendré).
4. Advice: yo que tú, yo en tu lugar
Yo en tu lugar, no diría nada.
Si yo fuera tú, iría a verlo.
“Yo que tú” is the most natural and most common in Spain. It sounds friendly, not like a lecture.
5. How to weigh up a decision
Expressions for comparing pros and cons:
On the one hand… on the other…
Lo bueno / lo malo es que…
The good / bad thing is that…
The good thing is that we’d be close to your family. The bad thing is that we’d be far from mine.

In October, Ana and Mihai spent a week in Bucharest. It was Ana’s first visit to the capital. Until then she had only known his grandfather’s village.
On the first day it rained non-stop. Ana looked out of the hotel window, saw the grey buildings and thought: “If everything were like this, I couldn’t live here.”
But she didn’t say anything. She had promised Mihai she would look at the city with open eyes, without deciding on the first day.

On the second day the sun came out. Mihai took her to Herăstrău Park, by the lake. The trees were red and gold, and there were families out for a walk, children on bikes and grandfathers playing chess.
“If we lived here, we’d come every Sunday,” said Mihai.
“If we lived here, I’d have to learn chess to talk to the grandfathers,” Ana answered, laughing.
On the third day, Mihai had his interview at the hospital. Ana was left on her own and decided to do a test: to spend the whole day without speaking English or Spanish.
She went to a bakery. She pointed at a plaited loaf and said, very slowly: “Bună ziua. Un… cozonac, vă rog.” (Good day. A… cozonac, please.)
The baker, an elderly woman with a headscarf, smiled from ear to ear and answered with a very, very long sentence of which Ana understood absolutely nothing.
All Ana could say was: “Sunt spaniolă.” (I’m Spanish.) And then something magical happened: the baker started speaking more slowly, with gestures, pointing at each thing and saying its name.
“Pâine” (bread). “Covrig” (pretzel). “Plăcintă” (pie). Ana repeated every word. Many were similar to Spanish: “pâine” was like “pan”, “lapte” like “leche”… well, more or less.
Half an hour later, Ana left the bakery with a cozonac, three covrigi, a free plăcintă and the feeling that, if she stayed, she could learn.
Meanwhile, at the hospital, Mihai was meeting his possible team. They were young, hard-working and very tired doctors. They showed him the wards, the old equipment and the corridors full of patients.
A young doctor told him: “If you came, you’d be the first head of department who has worked abroad. We need someone to show us how things are done elsewhere.”
Mihai felt something he hadn’t expected: responsibility. In Madrid he was one doctor among many. Here he could change something.
That evening they had dinner at a small restaurant in the centre. Ana told him about the bakery. Mihai told her about the hospital. Then they fell silent for a while.
“Well?” Mihai finally asked. “If you had to decide right now, what would you say?”
Ana took a while to answer. She thought about her mother, Grandma Rosario, the children in her class, the club. She also thought about the baker, the park, the tired doctors.
“If you’d asked me on Monday, I’d have said no. Today… I don’t know. And that scares me, because it means it’s possible.”
Mihai took her hand across the table.
“I have an idea. What if it wasn’t for ever? What if it was just two years? Long enough to help the team, for you to learn Romanian, for my grandfather to get to know you properly…”
“After that we’d go back to Madrid. Or not. We’d decide then, together.”
Ana gave him a long look. Then she took one of the covrigi out of her bag, broke it in two and gave him a piece.
“Two years,” she said. “But on one condition: if at any point one of us isn’t happy, we go back. No arguments.”
“Deal,” said Mihai, and took a bite of the covrig.
The next day, Mihai called the hospital. He told them he accepted, but that he couldn’t start until March: first he had a lot of things to wrap up in Madrid.
And then he made the hardest phone call of all. Not to his boss in Madrid. Not to his parents.
On the other end there was a long silence. Then a voice trying to sound cheerful: “If you leave, who’s going to eat my ramen experiments on Tuesdays?”

Mihai laughed, although he had a lump in his throat. “Tuesdays, on video call,” he promised. “And when you come to Bucharest, I’ll take you to the headscarf lady’s bakery. If you try her cozonac, maybe you’ll stay too.”
